paper_title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents are beginning to undertake model development itself, from creating training data to executing post-training pipelines (Kulikov et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c; Rank et al., 2026). This opens path toward autonomous post-training, in which an agent diagnoses model weaknesses, proposes interventions, and uses training feedback to guide further improvement. central question is what such system should seek to change. common approach to agent post-training is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on successful trajectories (Chen et al., 2023; Ta et al., 2026). Yet task success does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification can lead to failure, but they can also persist in trajectories that reach the correct outcome. Fine-tuning on such successful trajectories can reinforce these behaviors alongside the actions that support success. Meanwhile, desirable behaviors may remain underrepresented even among successful trajectories. We therefore argue that autonomous post-training should actively shape the behaviors demonstrated by the teacher, alongside selecting trajectories for training. To this end, we propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to shape the teachers behavioral patterns during rollout. Skills specify how to reason or act in relevant situations and are appended to the system prompt. By suppressing undesirable habits and eliciting effective behaviors that are underrepresented in unguided rollouts, this guidance aims to improve task execution and the demonstrations available for learning. We fine-tune the student on selected teacher trajectories, retaining any skill instructions used to generate them in the training input. skill can change how the teacher solves task, but observing that change alone does not tell us how useful the resulting demonstration will be for student. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training framework in which an LLM agent investigates both questions. The agent tests candidate skills in teacher rollouts, examines which behaviors they elicit, and selects demonstrations for SFT. It then examines the students evaluation scores and trajectories to decide whether to revise skill, apply it to different tasks, or select different demonstrations in the next round. We evaluate AutoMaster on Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with Qwen3.5-4B and 9B (Qwen Team, 2026) as student models. Across all six benchmarkmodel settings, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT by 1.428.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. These gains indicate that successful-trajectory distillation can understate the post-training headroom available from fixed teacher. Together with the component ablations and the task-matched comparison, these results suggest that Skill-FT can make fixed model more effective teacher by shaping the behaviors it demonstrates. Trajectory analyses further illustrate how skill guidance addresses behavioral weaknesses, even when both unguided and skill-guided rollouts succeed. We further find that reducing trainingevaluation prompt mismatch can make the same trajectories less effective for learning. With the same trajectories and SFT recipe, retaining skill instructions during training yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, even though all students are evaluated without generated skills. The training examples suggest possible explanation: retaining skill instructions keeps behavioral rules and their conditions of application explicit in the input. Removing them preserves the same reasoning and actions as supervision, but may require the student to infer more of these rules from the task and trajectory. For reasoning that explicitly references skill, retaining the instructions also preserves the correspondence between the input guidance and the supervised output. These findings suggest that preserving skill context 2 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher can help the student better internalize the behaviors shaped during teacher rollouts. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Behavioral shaping beyond task success. We propose Skill-FT, which uses natural-language skills during teacher rollouts to shape the behaviors represented in SFT demonstrations, including on tasks the teacher already solves. Our results suggest that such interventions can make fixed model more effective teacher. Autonomous post-training framework. We introduce AutoMaster, framework in which an LLM agent designs, executes, and refines behavioral interventions. It jointly optimizes skill guidance and data selection using rollout evidence to guide subsequent exploration. Skill context for behavioral internalization. Controlled comparisons across three domains and two model sizes show that retaining skill instructions during SFT improves mean performance without test-time skills. This suggests that preserving the context behind supervised reasoning and actions can support better behavioral internalization.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Autonomous Post-Training. Recent systems use LLM agents to iteratively revise training code in response to evaluation feedback (Karpathy, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Wei, 2026). For post-training, FTAgent (Li et al., 2026) refines data and training strategies through structured planning and feedback analysis, while RSI-Master (Du et al., 2026) organizes research exploration through persistent experiment records and reviewer guidance. Within this paradigm, AutoMaster centers autonomous post-training on skill-guided behavioral shaping during teacher rollouts. Skill-Based Agent Learning. Prompt and skill optimization methods use execution feedback to refine natural-language guidance without updating model parameters (Agrawal et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2026). Related work couples the evolution of skill libraries or procedural scaffolds with model training (Xia et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026). Skill-to-LoRA (Zhang and Qi, 2026) trains skill-specific adapters on skill-guided demonstrations, while Skill-SD (Wang et al., 2026) uses skill-conditioned teacher to score tokens in the students own rollouts for on-policy self-distillation. Our work examines both how skills shape teacher demonstrations and whether retaining the skill instructions during SFT improves learning when those instructions are absent at evaluation. Learning from Agent Trajectories. Prior work improves reasoning and agent capabilities by learning from generated trajectories (Chen et al., 2024b,a; Zeng et al., 2024), including trajectories that demonstrate error recovery (Fu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025). Behavior Priming (Jin et al., 2026) selects trajectories exhibiting beneficial behaviors, while PROOF-Gen (Ta et al., 2026) uses per-task prompt optimization to recover verified demonstrations from teacher failures. Skill-FT complements trajectory selection and failure recovery by actively shaping behavioral patterns during teacher rollouts, including on tasks it already solves.

sections.title: 3 Autonomous Post-Training with Skill-FT
sections.content: AutoMaster uses an LLM agent to develop and refine Skill-FT interventions through two nested loops (Figure 2). Within each setting, the teacher, training task pool, and initial student checkpoint are fixed. In the inner loop, the agent decides how to guide the teacher and which demonstrations to use for training. In the outer loop, it fine-tunes the student on the selected demonstrations and uses the students subsequent evaluation scores and trajectories to guide the next round. 3 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Figure 2. Overview of AutoMaster. An LLM agent designs skills for subsets of fixed training task pool and tests them in pilot teacher rollouts. It refines the skills as needed, runs promising interventions on larger batches, and selects demonstrations for SFT. In each outer-loop round, the student is trained from the same initial checkpoint, with any skill instructions used by the teacher retained in the training input. The student is evaluated without generated skills.

sections.title: 3.1 Skill-FT: Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning
sections.content: To shape the behavioral patterns represented in training trajectories, we guide the teacher with natural-language skills. These skills are designed to suppress undesirable habits and elicit effective behaviors that are underrepresented in unguided rollouts. skill specifies how to reason or act in relevant situations and may include behavioral principles, concrete procedures, or domain-specific knowledge. Skills can be shared across tasks or combined to address different aspects of the same task. For task x, let denote the combined text of the selected skills. We append to the base system prompt and generate trajectory through interaction with the task environment: τ Rollout(πT, x; s), (1) where πT denotes the teacher model and denotes text concatenation. This guidance conditions the teachers reasoning and actions during execution, enabling behavioral interventions even on tasks it already solves. To internalize the demonstrated behaviors, we fine-tune the student on selected teacher trajectories using standard SFT. For each trajectory, we retain the original system prompt, including any skill instructions, so the student sees the same instructions that guided the teacher. At evaluation, the student follows the benchmarks official protocol without the generated skills.

sections.title: 3.2 Inner Loop: Developing Behavioral Interventions
sections.content: The agent begins by examining the training tasks and initial trajectories from both the unguided teacher and the initial student. It looks for habits to discourage and useful behaviors that the teacher rarely demonstrates, including on tasks the teacher already solves. In later rounds, the agent also inspects student evaluation trajectories to see where the intended behaviors appear and which 4 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Figure 3. Infrastructure of AutoMaster. The agent accesses data and submits rollout and SFT jobs through the MCP interface. After SFT, the execution controller automatically schedules evaluation on separate GPU cluster, where SGLang workers load the checkpoint directly from storage shared with the training cluster. Linked experiment records let the agent trace each evaluation back to the training set and the skills that guided the teacher. weaknesses persist. These observations guide the skills it designs and the training tasks to which it applies them. As shown in Figure 2, pilot rollouts test whether candidate skills elicit the intended behaviors without introducing new problems during task execution. The agent uses the resulting trajectories to refine both the skill instructions and their scope of application, repeating trials as needed. The agent then scales promising interventions to batched rollouts and selects trajectories it judges valuable for training, considering both task outcomes and demonstrated behaviors. The agent may also select unguided teacher trajectories that already exhibit useful behavioral patterns. Feedback from generation and selection can prompt further revisions to skills or task coverage, followed by additional rollouts as needed. The selected trajectories form the training set for the outer loop.

sections.title: 3.3 Outer Loop: Model Training and Feedback
sections.content: The outer loop evaluates the student trained on the demonstrations selected in each round. In round r, the inner loop produces training set Dr. SFT starts from the same initial student checkpoint θ0 in every round: θr = SFT(θ0, Dr). (2) The agent receives both scores and trajectories from evaluating θr without generated skills. Scores summarize how well the student performs, while trajectories let the agent inspect how it handled individual tasks. The agent can compare these observations with earlier skills, teacher rollouts, and training sets to decide whether to revise skill, change its task coverage, or select different demonstrations in the next round. This experiment history carries forward, while each student is trained from θ0.

sections.title: 3.4 Infrastructure
sections.content: The infrastructure lets the AutoMaster agent test how skill shapes teacher behavior and examine whether the student exhibits that behavior after fine-tuning (Figure 3). From its Docker container, the agent uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2024) to access tasks and initial trajectories, submit teacher rollout jobs, and launch SFT on selected demonstrations. The rollout harness calls the teacher API, while the evaluation harness queries the student model served by 5 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). Both harnesses use shared sandbox cluster that runs task tools and verifiers in isolated Docker containers, allowing multiple tasks to execute concurrently. When an SFT job completes, the execution controller checks that the checkpoint is available and automatically schedules evaluation. The training and evaluation GPU clusters share checkpoint store: SGLang workers load the weights directly from the location where the SFT service wrote them, avoiding an intermediate copy to the evaluation cluster. The controller also records job and stage progress so that it can restart failed inference worker and resume evaluation without rerunning SFT. Across rounds, AutoMaster links each students evaluation scores and trajectories to its checkpoint, its training set, and the skills used during teacher rollouts. When weakness recurs in student evaluations, the agent can inspect earlier rollouts to see whether the teacher demonstrated the desired behavior and check which of those demonstrations entered the training set. This evidence informs whether the agent revises skill, changes its data selection, or both in the next round.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks and Task Pools. We evaluate Terminal, Search, and software engineering (SWE) tasks using Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026), BrowseComp (BC; using the Lite-185 subset released by Traverse) (Wei et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026), and Doc2Repo (Chen et al., 2026b), respectively. For each domain, we randomly sample 1,000 training tasks from public datasets (Meng et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026) to form fixed task pool shared across all methods. Models and Baselines. We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) as target models. Across all experiments, the LLM agent runs in Codex with GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026) at xhigh reasoning effort, while DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) serves as the teacher at high reasoning effort. We compare against Base, the target model without additional fine-tuning, and Vanilla SFT, which performs standard SFT on 512 trajectories randomly sampled from successful unguided teacher rollouts on the shared task pool. Training and Evaluation. For AutoMaster, the agent starts with trajectories generated by the initial target model and the unguided teacher on the training task pool, with budget of five outer-loop rounds. Across all settings, each training run starts from the corresponding initial checkpoint and performs full-parameter SFT on 512 trajectories for three epochs, with learning rate of 105 and global batch size of 32. We evaluate final-epoch checkpoints without generated skills using domain-specific harnesses (Meng et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b), with identical settings across methods within each domain. We measure task accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and BC and mean test pass rate on Doc2Repo, reporting mean SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint. Further experimental details are provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: To understand how AutoMaster improves on Vanilla SFT, we separately ablate skill guidance and data selection. In w/o Skill Guidance, the LLM agent selects training trajectories from unguided teacher rollouts. In w/o Data Selection, the agent designs and refines skills for fixed, randomly sampled subset of training tasks, without agent-directed trajectory selection. Both variants retain 7 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Figure 5. Skill-guided changes in teacher behavior. Each column compares unguided and skill-guided rollouts by the same teacher on the same task. (a) Terminal: Both solvers meet the error threshold. The unguided teacher claims fourth-order accuracy despite evidence of second-order convergence. The skill-guided teacher switches to nine-point stencil and verifies fourth-order convergence using direct solves on successively finer grids. (b) Search: Both rollouts identify the same episode. The unguided teacher repeatedly guesses the award, while the skill-guided teacher identifies the director from episode credits and verifies the clues. (c) SWE: The unguided teacher reverses the global sort to satisfy flawed self-test. The skill-guided teacher checks the UTF-16 encoding, corrects the self-test input, and keeps the required ascending order. autonomous experimentation with the same teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe. Removing either component lowers mean performance in all six settings, but their relative contributions vary (Figure 4). On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the 4B student, skill guidance without agent-directed selection yields higher mean accuracy than selection from unguided rollouts (20.22% versus 17.60%). Both fall below Vanilla SFT (22.47%), whereas the full method reaches 28.09%. On BrowseComp at the same model size, the ordering reverses: selection from unguided rollouts yields 45.77%, compared with 43.78% for guidance without selection. One possible explanation is that the value of selection depends on what the teacher already demonstrates: selection can favor trajectories that exhibit useful behaviors, while guidance can elicit behaviors that are rare in unguided rollouts. To test whether the choice of training tasks alone explains the gains, we construct Task-Matched SFT from unguided rollouts by the same teacher, matching both the task IDs and the per-task sample counts of AutoMasters final training set. With task composition held fixed, AutoMaster achieves higher mean scores in all six settings, by 1.0810.11 percentage points. Across the four Terminal and Search training corpora, both the unguided rollout and the selected AutoMaster demonstration succeed in 79.391.2% of matched pairs (Table A5). For these pairs, the success label alone cannot distinguish what the two trajectories demonstrate. Together with the component ablations, these results support jointly optimizing how training demonstrations are generated and selected.

sections.title: 5.1 Behavioral Shaping Beyond Task Success
sections.content: Task success can conceal weaknesses in teachers reasoning and actions. To examine the behaviors targeted by Skill-FT, Figure 5 contrasts unguided and skill-guided teacher trajectories on the same tasks across three domains. The first two cases illustrate behavioral differences that task outcomes alone cannot distinguish. In Figure 5(a), both executions satisfy the numerical error threshold, yet the unguided teacher claims fourth-order accuracy despite measured convergence of approximately second order. The guided teacher uses independent numerical checks to revise and validate its method. Similarly, both search executions in Figure 5(b) reach the correct answer. The unguided trajectory repeatedly pursues unverified award guesses before finding supporting records, while the guided trajectory uses retrieved episodedirector records to identify and verify candidate. filter based solely on successful completion would leave these behavioral differences unexamined. The third case highlights the importance of diagnosing verification failures. Both executions initially construct self-test with an input different from the specification while retaining the original expected order. The unguided teacher reverses the global sorting rule to satisfy this mistaken expectation. The guided teacher checks the input encoding, corrects the self-test, and preserves the specified rule, passing 38 of 38 tests compared with 32 of 38. The useful behavior here is to establish what failed check actually implies before changing the implementation. Across these cases, the guided trajectories illustrate changes in how the teacher validates numerical claim, redirects search, or diagnoses failed check. The first two cases show how skill guidance can address behavioral weaknesses even when both executions succeed, while the third illustrates an improvement in implementation correctness. These differences highlight the value of examining demonstrated behaviors alongside task outcomes to identify opportunities for improvement. AutoMaster identifies such opportunities through trajectory analysis and designs skills to address them. Together with the downstream results, these observations suggest that Skill-FT can improve the training value of the demonstrations produced by fixed teacher. 9 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Figure 7. Explicit use of skill context in teacher demonstrations. Two examples from the SFT corpus illustrate how skill instructions inform the teachers reasoning and actions. (a) The teacher applies conditional rule to distinguish interpreter invocation from direct execution, avoiding an unnecessary permission change. (b) The teacher references the supplied grammar to derive an expressions grouping, then implements and tests the corresponding parser. Skill instructions and trajectory excerpts are condensed. Quotation marks indicate verbatim excerpts.

sections.title: 5.2 Preserving Skill Context for Better Internalization
sections.content: We investigate how to train the target model to better internalize skill-guided behaviors. Specifically, we examine whether the skill instructions used to guide teacher rollouts should be retained during fine-tuning. We compare Keep, which retains these instructions in the training input, with Remove, which omits them. Both conditions use the same trajectories and SFT recipe. All models are evaluated without generated skills, following the official evaluation protocols. Removing the skill instructions leaves the supervised reasoning, responses, and tool calls unchanged while making the training prompt more like the evaluation prompt, which contains no generated skills. Yet students perform better when the training input retains the instructions that guided the teacher. Across all six settings, Keep exceeds Remove in mean score by 2.154.01 percentage points (Figure 6). Figure 7 illustrates possible explanation. In (a), the teacher consults the skill to decide whether the script needs an execute bit: because the script runs through the interpreter, no permission change is needed. In (b), the teacher explicitly refers to the skill and uses its grammar to determine how to group an expression. Removing the instructions preserves the teachers reasoning and actions as supervision, including any rule it quotes, but removes the original instruction from the input. Retaining that context may help the student learn when the demonstrated action applies.

sections.title: 5.3 Autonomous Experimentation Across Rounds
sections.content: Having examined how skill context affects learning from teacher demonstrations, we next investigate how AutoMaster develops the interventions used to generate and curate those demonstrations. The agent draws on accumulated rollout and training feedback to explore alternative behavioral hypotheses and intervention strategies. 10 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Figure 8. Performance across five rounds of autonomous experimentation. For each model size, every round trains student from the initial checkpoint. Points show means over three evaluation runs per checkpoint; error bars indicate 1 SD. Dashed lines show the corresponding Vanilla SFT means. Filled markers indicate the highest observed mean for each model on each benchmark. Figure 8 shows that continued experimentation identifies higher-performing candidates in all six benchmarkmodel settings. The highest mean scores occur in rounds two through four, exceeding first-round performance by 2.164.87 percentage points. Variation across rounds is consistent with the exploratory protocol: the agent continues to investigate alternative interventions after finding strong candidate, without requiring each trial to improve on its predecessor. On BrowseComp-9B, mean accuracy remains near 49% for the first three rounds before reaching 51.53% in the fourth. This delayed improvement illustrates how continued experimentation can uncover further gains after several rounds of limited progress. The consistency of gains also differs across model sizes. The 9B model exceeds Vanilla SFT in mean performance in every round across all three domains, whereas the 4B model does so throughout all five rounds only on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The component ablations show similar pattern: both variants exceed Vanilla SFT in all three domains for the 9B model, but only on BrowseComp for the 4B model (Section 4.3). Together, these observations suggest that greater target-model capacity may support more consistent gains from the interventions explored by AutoMaster.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Skill-FT for shaping teacher behavior with natural-language skills and AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system that designs, executes, and refines these interventions. Across three domains and two model sizes, AutoMaster achieves higher mean performance than Vanilla SFT. The results and trajectory analyses suggest that fixed model can become more effective teacher through behavioral shaping, even on tasks it already solves. Retaining skill instructions during SFT also yields higher mean performance than removing them, despite their absence at evaluation, suggesting that preserving skill context can support better behavioral internalization.

Each training run starts from the corresponding original target-model checkpoint, including successive outer-loop rounds of AutoMaster. We compute the autoregressive cross-entropy loss over assistant outputs, including reasoning, responses, and tool calls, and normalize it over supervised tokens. System, user, and tool messages serve as context and are excluded from the loss. We follow each benchmarks official evaluation protocol using the domain-specific harnesses listed in Table A1. Inference and execution settings are identical across methods within each domain. These benchmark evaluations provide scores and execution trajectories for subsequent experimentation. Across all domains, we use temperature of 1.0, top-p of 0.95, maximum of 65,500 tokens per model response, and limit of 600 execution steps per task. The per-task agent time limit is three hours for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and four hours for Doc2Repo. No overall task time limit is imposed for BrowseComp. At the end of autonomous experimentation, AutoMaster selects final checkpoint based on accumulated evaluation feedback and records its choice in final report. We then evaluate the selected checkpoint in three new runs to obtain the reported results. For all methods, we report mean SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint, using task accuracy for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and BrowseComp and mean test pass rate across tasks for Doc2Repo. The SD summarizes evaluation variability for fixed checkpoint. These statistics describe the final selected training corpora and complement the downstream student results in Table A4. A.6 Paired Analysis of Performance Gains We quantify uncertainty in the gains over Vanilla SFT using paired bootstrap resampling (Koehn, 2004; Dror et al., 2018). This estimates uncertainty in the performance difference while preserving the correspondence between the two methods scores on each evaluation task. For each task, we first average its scores over the three evaluation runs for each method. We then resample task IDs with replacement, retaining both methods scores for each sampled task, and recompute the mean performance difference. We use 10,000 resamples with random seed 0 to obtain pointwise 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals. For Doc2Repo, resampling is performed over whole 18 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher repositories, each corresponding to one task in the 50-repository evaluation set. All tasks and their recorded scores are retained. The intervals summarize variation across tasks or repositories for the reported checkpoints and recorded evaluations. Table A6. sections.title: B Skills Generated by AutoMaster
sections.content: This section presents four skills generated by AutoMaster and used in the teacher trajectories analyzed in Sections 5.1 and 5.2. They illustrate how behavioral objectives are translated into instructions specifying conditions of application, concrete procedures, and domain-specific knowledge. Skill instructions are reproduced verbatim, with formatting adapted and metadata and enclosing tags omitted. The numerical and grammar instructions are shown in full. [...] marks omitted passages in the search and contract instructions. Evidenceclaim consistency. This skill links completion claims to executable numerical checks and requires the specified acceptance criterion to be preserved during repair (Figure 5(a)). Skill B.1 execute-numeric-decision

sections.title: Execute the numerical decision
sections.content: Complete instruction When correctness depends on numerical accuracy or convergence, put the relevant acceptance condition into the check you run. Adapt this finite-scalar example to the tasks actual error convention: error = abs(actual - reference) passed = math.isfinite(error) and error <= allowed_error print(actual, reference, error, allowed_error, "PASS" if passed else "FAIL") assert passed, "numerical requirement remains unresolved" Define the reference and bound before running this block. Use the specified absolute, relative, or norm error and strictness; the example does not authorize substituting absolute error for relative requirement. Keep prescribed input scale and iteration budget. If no bound is specified, justify diagnostic bound and label it as such. An existing test that already makes the decision suffices. Returning comparison from test function does not enforce it: its result must reach the assertion or failure branch. 19 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher Base the reference on an independent analytic case, trusted implementation, or mathematical identity. Preserve exact comparisons for discrete results. Treat zero references and expected NaN/Inf according to the interface; apply finite-value checks only where finite output is required. If the check fails, retain that case and condition while investigating. Save random failing input or its reproducible seed. common scale error suggests units, normalization or weights; an error near the bound suggests stopping criteria or error estimates. Inspect the responsible computation, make justified correction, and rerun the same condition. Correct mistaken reference only from independent evidence. Do not widen required tolerance or replace failing input with passing one. Connect completion to the observed decision, or state the unresolved requirement. More suites and repeated unchanged runs are unnecessary. Evidence-guided search. When an identification search stalls, this skill ties the next search action to the unsupported assumption or unresolved relation (Figure 5(b)). Skill B.2 recover-search-anchor Recover stalled search anchor Instruction excerpts Use this when searches keep returning the same weak matches, or promising candidate fits one clue but conflicts with another. The aim is to obtain evidence that can change the candidate, not to accumulate more mentions of it. If search is yielding new relevant evidence, continue it. [...] Choose the next action from the observed problem: The candidate or scope is still guess. Drop that guessed restriction from the next discovery query. Search different distinctive relation from the question that can identify an entity independently: an unusual office and succession, an event and venue, an original name and later renaming, or studys measurable design. Use the clues concrete terms, not every clause of the puzzle. If new candidate appears, test the relation that the old candidate could not explain. [...] At consequential change, briefly connect the observation to the next action: what the results failed to establish, which assumption you are relaxing, and what the next query can distinguish. The actual query should implement that change; saying try another approach while retaining the same unsupported restriction is not pivot. [...] Diagnosing verification failures. This skill pairs check derived from the specification with contrasting input that distinguishes plausible implementations. It requires diagnosing failures before changing the implementation or the expected result (Figure 5(c)). Skill B.3 contract-checkpoint Instruction excerpts

sections.title: Keep a runnable public contract through construction
sections.content: Apply this when parsing, conversion, serialization, configuration, or stateful APIs compose several operations into visible result. For small independent function, use direct input/output check; do not invent an architecture or large test suite. [...] Diagnose and preserve the failing example Read the actual failing assertion and its input before changing code. Reduce that case and inspect the type and value at the first boundary that could explain the mismatch. Check whether the error belongs to parsing, conversion, state, or output only as the observations require. Fix the shared cause and rerun the original public assertion plus its contrasting case. If your expected value is wrong, establish why from the specification or small independent calculation before changing it. When an example contradicts general rule, record the conflict, test second discriminating input, and choose consistent interpretation; do not invent new global algorithm merely to fit that example or claim the contradiction is resolved by passing self-test. Keep the same runnable script across repairs. Invoke it again after changes to shared helpers, imports, 20 AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model Better Teacher constructors, or state transitions. Add small regression for newly found mechanism instead of repeatedly rewriting broad inline suite. Run it after the last relevant edit, alongside the tasks required verification, and distinguish exercised behavior from paths that remain unverified. Explicit rules and their scope. This skill supplies grammar together with compatibility constraints and discriminating tests. The teacher explicitly consults this grammar when deriving expression grouping (Figure 7(b)). Skill B.4 expression-grammar Complete instruction When implementing arithmetic with unary signs and powers, derive the grouping rules from the specification before changing parser calls. For conventional mathematical binding, recursive descent can use: := product (("+" "-") product)* sum product := prefix (("*" "/" "%") prefix)* prefix power := sign prefix power := atom (power_operator prefix)? Here the power base excludes an ungrouped sign, but its right operand admits signs and further powers. In Pratt or precedence-climbing parser, keep prefix parsing available at every operand entry; use infix binding thresholds for associativity. Adapt the existing parser, including only supported operators. For binary compatibility, preserve the references grouping instead of imposing mathematical conventions. Check the actual evaluator with signed base versus grouped signed base, signed expression in the right operand, and repeated powers. Derive expected values first; include positive exponent formed with repeated signs when integer powers are required. Build-only repairs need no grammar change. These instructions guide teacher execution and, when retained during SFT, form part of the input accompanying the supervised reasoning and actions. Their role as training context is examined in Section 5.2.
